paras: The Mount Vernon trolley strike and coercion of Black replacement workers took place on May 5, 1903, when striking Italian laborers in Mount Vernon, New York, drove a gang of Black workers from their trenches and compelled them to join the strikers' union. No one was reported killed or injured, and the strike was settled ten days later on the strikers' terms. New York papers headlined that the Black workers had joined the union "in Terror of Death," while wire copy said they had been "persuaded."

About 250 Italian laborers employed by the New York contractor T. E. Crimmins to relay the tracks of the Union trolley road had been on strike since the previous week. They demanded $1.50 a day for eight hours' work instead of ten, and belonged, according to the Sun, to the new Rockmen and Excavators' Union (a wire report said the "Dirt Diggers' union"). To replace them, a gang of about fifty "Southern negroes" was brought to Mount Vernon during the night and put to work on First Street.

On the morning of May 5 the strikers, armed with clubs and pickaxes, came to the First Street trenches and swarmed about them. The Black workers fled, leaving their picks and shovels behind, and nearly all of them were later marched to the strikers' headquarters, where they were made to join the union and take an oath of loyalty. The Black men said they had joined because they feared they would lose their lives if they refused, and they could not take part in union meetings, which were held in Italian.

The strikers then moved through Mount Vernon and Pelham, driving other gangs from street work on South Columbus Avenue and at the Pelham reservoir. At Corcoran Manor about 150 of them gathered before the home of the contractor William Archer, whose foreman said they had threatened to kill him and his men if they did not join the strike. Police Chief Foley, revolver drawn, arrested the strike leader, who gave his name as Louis Demarti, and officers drove the strikers into Pelham.

Demarti was charged with inciting a riot and resisting arrest; no report of a trial was found. Crimmins planned to bring in a carload of Black workers the next day, and every policeman and deputy in the city was ordered to report at 7 a.m. A May 9 dispatch said eleven of fifteen replacement men, "most of whom are negroes," were so scared by strikers that they left for New York; four worked under police guard.

On May 15 Edward Maher, president of the Union Railway Company, settled the strike by granting the demands after the contractors failed to put men to work by a 1 o'clock deadline he had set. The New-York Tribune noted that Black workers put to work during the strike had been "frightened off" and that the railroad's foreman, Timothy Meehan, hired all the Italians he could find "but he would not employ any negroes."

The first reports came by wire on May 5, when the Washington Evening Star and the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican placed Mount Vernon in a roundup of strike disorder around New York under headlines such as "More Strike Rioting" and "Workmen Intimidated." That wire, repeated in the Barre Daily Times the next day, said the strikers had "persuaded" sixty Black workers to quit and closed on a police guard at a separate sewer job.

The New York Sun and New-York Tribune carried a fuller Mount Vernon dispatch on May 6 that made the Black workers central, under the headlines "Italians Take Mount Vernon" and "Make Negroes Join It." Both called the strikers a "mob" that left residents in terror and the police powerless, and the Sun ended with the Black workers' own explanation. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The wire put the strikers at between 300 and 400 and the Black workers at sixty, while the Sun and Tribune gave 250 strikers and about fifty Black workers. On how the Black workers came to join, the local dispatch, with its sequence of flight, march and forced oath, is more detailed than the wire's "persuaded."

reader.title: Mount Vernon trolley strike and coercion of Black replacement workers
bases: Italian trolley-track laborers on strike drove replacement and other workers from their jobs, compelling Black replacement workers to quit and join their union, in a wage-and-hours strike that ended with the demands granted (A1, A5, A8).

A wire report (A1, A6) and a separate local dispatch (A5, with the Tribune's version A3-A4) agree that striking Italians made a gang of Black workers quit and join the strike on May 5, and a later report (A8) confirms that Black replacements were frightened off.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Between 300 and 400 Italian strikers marched to where sixty negroes were working and 'persuaded' them to quit and join the strike, then got nearly all laborers in the city to quit.

accounts.label: Mount Vernon dispatch (Sun, Tribune)
accounts.gist: About 250 armed strikers swarmed the First Street trenches; the terrified Black workers fled and were later marched to strike headquarters and compelled to join the union and swear loyalty.

accounts.label: Black workers' statement
accounts.gist: As relayed by the Sun, the Black workers said they joined only because they feared they would be killed if they refused.

framing.detail: The wire placed Mount Vernon in a roundup of strike disorder ('More Strike Rioting', 'Workmen Intimidated') and described the Black workers as 'persuaded' to join.

The New York Sun and Tribune framed the strikers as a mob that took the city ('Italians Take Mount Vernon', 'Make Negroes Join It'), stressing terror among residents and the Black workers' fear of death.

conflicts.note: The local Sun dispatch is the more detailed source; the gap is small.
The local papers and the settlement report agree on 250.

conflicts.field: how the Black workers came to join

versions.value: fled in terror, then compelled to join the union and take an oath

conflicts.note: The local dispatch gives the sequence and the workers' own stated reason (fear for their lives); the wire compresses it.
Probably different names for the same body; neither paper reconciles them.

record_check.dossier: An unnamed gang of about fifty (local) or sixty (wire) Black replacement workers; later fifteen replacements, most of them Black
Striking Italian laborers of contractor T. E. Crimmins (Rockmen and Excavators' / 'Dirt Diggers'' union); leader Louis Demarti arrested

armed_gathering, threat and work_action are supported; 'driven_out' fits only in the sense of being run off a work site; 'seizure' is not supported beyond the workers being marched to strike headquarters

Coverage runs to 1903-05-16 (A7, A8); no Black-press coverage found
